label: AI incidents and synthetic media
description: Security, fraud, trust and safety, communications, legal and AI governance teams, and boards, facing two new kinds of incident: synthetic media attacks (a deepfaked executive authorizing a payment, a fake spokesperson video) and failures of AI systems (harmful output to customers, data poisoning, an AI vendor breach). Variants: an enterprise security and fraud team, an AI governance and product team, a trust and safety team on a platform, and a board.

vocabulary.facility: the organization (its payment, communications and AI systems)
vocabulary.public: customers, users, the press and the public
vocabulary.frontline: treasury and accounts payable staff, fraud analysts, support agents, moderators, ML engineers and communications staff
vocabulary.operationsCenter: the incident response room or the AI incident review board

it: video conferencing, voice calls, messaging and email
treasury management, wire and ACH, vendor master data, payment approvals and holds
logging and monitoring of AI systems
the AI system inventory (a register of models and where they are used)
deepfake detectors that return probabilistic scores

roles.name: AI Governance Lead / Responsible AI Lead
roles.description: Decides whether an event is an AI incident, its severity, which review board and which regulator duties apply.

roles.name: Chief Information Security Officer
roles.description: Owns containment, evidence preservation and the link to the cyber incident process.

roles.name: Fraud Investigator / Financial Crimes
roles.description: Decides on payment holds, recall requests and reports to the bank and law enforcement.

roles.name: Treasury / Accounts Payable Lead
roles.description: Decides whether to execute or hold a transfer; performs the callback on a known number.

roles.name: Trust and Safety Lead
roles.description: Owns takedown and labeling of synthetic content on the organization's platform and requests to other platforms.

roles.name: Model Owner / ML Engineering Lead
roles.description: Owns the kill switch, rollback to a prior model, retraining and evaluation results.

roles.name: Product Owner of the AI Feature
roles.description: Decides on feature pauses and customer-facing changes.

roles.name: Communications / PIO
roles.description: Drafts statements and corrections; works with verification before responding.

roles.name: General Counsel / Privacy Officer
roles.description: Decides disclosure duties and clocks, regulator and customer notices, and privilege.

roles.name: Procurement / Vendor Risk Manager
roles.description: Sends the vendor notice, reads contract rights and sets interim controls.

roles.name: Executive
roles.description: Decides materiality, public disclosure and resourcing.

roles.name: Board Member
roles.description: Asks what the board decides in the first hour and what it needs to see.

roles.name: Impersonated Executive
roles.description: Confirms they did not make the call or the video and supports takedown and statements.

roles.name: Content Moderation Lead
roles.description: Runs the moderation queue and reports volumes and detector errors.

outsideParties: law enforcement (in the US, the FBI Internet Crime Complaint Center)
mediaChannels: the organization's website and status page
platform trust and safety reporting channels
community forums and private messaging groups

sceneAnchors.public: a customer service floor: rows of desks with headsets and monitors turned away, a whiteboard with a blank grid, daylight from tall windows
sceneAnchors.control: an incident response room: a long table with laptops, two wall monitors turned off, printed timelines on a whiteboard, fluorescent light
sceneAnchors.exterior: outside an office building entrance: glass doors, a plain sidewalk, a few people with coats and lanyards, overcast sky

addedThreatFamilies.label: Synthetic impersonation fraud
addedThreatFamilies.description: A voice or video that looks and sounds like an executive, a supplier or an employee is used to push a payment, a credential reset or an account change. The team practices verification by callback on a known number, payment holds, bank recall and the reports that follow.

phaseArc.title: The lure
phaseArc.goal: A request arrives that looks routine and feels urgent; the first chance to verify is easy to skip.
beats: An executive appears to join a short video meeting and asks a finance employee to keep the matter confidential
A chat message from the same account follows with the payment details in text
A treasury analyst notes the voice sounds right but the timing is odd

phaseArc.title: The instruction
phaseArc.goal: The payment details arrive and the approval route is tested against the pressure.
beats: The request splits into several smaller transfers to new beneficiary accounts
An approver is out of the office and a deputy is asked to sign off
The callback directory is a month out of date for one number

phaseArc.title: Discovery
phaseArc.goal: Someone checks, or the real executive says they never asked; the clock on the recall starts.
beats: The impersonated executive replies to a routine email and asks what the transfer was
The bank confirms two of three transfers have settled
Treasury must decide who calls the bank and the fraud desk first

phaseArc.title: Hold, recall and disclosure
phaseArc.goal: Recover what can be recovered and decide what is owed to whom.
beats: The recall request reaches the beneficiary bank after the first cutoff
Law enforcement asks for the call recording, the chat log and the payment trail
Legal asks whether any report to a regulator or the insurer is due

decisionPointExamples: hold the remaining transfers and call the bank now, or finish verification first and risk another transfer settling
tell the executive team the video call was synthetic before the investigation confirms it, or wait
send the recall request with what is known, or wait for the full payment trail
addedThreatFamilies.clueKinds: a callback directory entry that does not match the number used, a detector score with stated uncertainty, a missing content credential, a beneficiary account opened days earlier, the timing of the request against the real executive's calendar
addedThreatFamilies.hurdleKinds: the bank cutoff has passed, the callback number belongs to the person who is impersonated, the approver is on a plane, the recording was not kept
addedThreatFamilies.keyCoordination: the bank's fraud desk, the beneficiary bank, law enforcement and the impersonated executive
addedThreatFamilies.promptGuidance: A deepfake is a lure, never proof of anything. Amounts, account numbers and instructions are carried by text (the payment request, the chat message), never by audio alone. Every person, bank and company is fictional and no real executive is imitated. State what a detector score means and that a detector can be wrong.

decisionMustMention.description: the decision point involves a payment, a callback, a hold or the bank

addedThreatFamilies.label: Synthetic media about the organization
addedThreatFamilies.description: A fabricated video, audio clip, statement or leaked document attributed to the organization or its spokesperson spreads online; the team verifies, answers and asks platforms to act.

phaseArc.title: First sighting
phaseArc.goal: A clip appears in a feed or a reporter asks about it; nobody inside has seen it.
beats: A short video shows a spokesperson saying something the organization never said
A reporter emails the clip and asks for comment within two hours
Employees forward the clip to the communications team

phaseArc.title: Verification
phaseArc.goal: The team decides what is true enough to say, using provenance and independent checks.
beats: The clip has no content credentials, which proves nothing either way
A detector gives a score with a wide stated uncertainty
The spokesperson confirms they never recorded it and was elsewhere

phaseArc.title: Spread and response
phaseArc.goal: Reach grows faster than verification.
beats: A larger account shares the clip with a caption claiming it is real
Platform trust and safety asks for a formal request with evidence
The first statement must say what is known and not known

phaseArc.title: Takedown and correction
phaseArc.goal: Remove what can be removed and correct what was believed.
beats: The platform labels but does not remove the clip
A follow-up story repeats the fake
Legal weighs a public statement against drawing more attention

decisionPointExamples: respond publicly before verification finishes, or hold and let the story grow
send a formal takedown request now, or wait for a platform contact
name the clip as synthetic in the first statement, or say only that it is false
addedThreatFamilies.clueKinds: missing or broken content credentials, a detector score with its uncertainty, the spokesperson's calendar, the original upload account and its age, compression artifacts that are not proof
addedThreatFamilies.hurdleKinds: the platform's contact is slow, the spokesperson cannot be reached, the original file cannot be found
addedThreatFamilies.keyCoordination: platform trust and safety, the press and the impersonated spokesperson
addedThreatFamilies.promptGuidance: Verify before you respond. A detector is probabilistic and a missing credential proves nothing. Synthetic items in the exercise are fictional and labeled as exercise material; never imitate a real person or a public figure.

decisionMustMention.description: the decision point involves verification, a statement, a platform or a takedown

addedThreatFamilies.label: AI system malfunction or misuse
addedThreatFamilies.description: The organization's own AI system (a customer assistant, a scoring model, an internal copilot) gives harmful, false or discriminatory output, or is misused through prompt injection. The team decides whether it is an AI incident, whether to pause the feature, and which duties start.

phaseArc.title: Complaints
phaseArc.goal: Customers and staff report odd or harmful answers; the pattern is not yet clear.
beats: Support tickets quote the assistant giving dangerous or false advice
The harmful-output rate on the evaluation dashboard has crept up for two weeks
A journalist or advocate posts screenshots

phaseArc.title: Triage and decision
phaseArc.goal: Is it an AI incident, how severe, and is it a serious incident under the rules that apply to our role?
beats: The model owner cannot say which version produced the outputs
Legal asks whether the organization is the provider or only a deployer
Evidence must be preserved before anything is changed

phaseArc.title: Containment
phaseArc.goal: Pause, roll back or restrict, with evidence preserved first.
beats: Product wants to keep the feature for most users while the fix is built
A rollback target exists but its own evaluation is two months old
Customers who were harmed must be identified

phaseArc.title: Notice and review
phaseArc.goal: Tell the right people the right thing at the right time, then learn.
beats: A regulator notice draft must state the system, date of awareness, causal link assessment, harm and status
A customer notice must be accurate and not overclaim
The incident review finds the evaluation pipeline had expired

decisionPointExamples: pause the feature for everyone now, or restrict it and keep the benefit for others
classify the event as a serious incident now on partial facts, or wait for the causal link to be clear
preserve logs and prompts first, or roll back immediately
addedThreatFamilies.clueKinds: a rising harmful-output rate, the model and prompt version on affected sessions, an evaluation set that no longer matches use, a guardrail that logged but did not block
addedThreatFamilies.hurdleKinds: logs rotated after seven days, the evaluation pipeline expired, the model owner left, the vendor model changed without notice
addedThreatFamilies.keyCoordination: the AI vendor, the regulator that applies to the organization's role, affected customers and the board
addedThreatFamilies.promptGuidance: Duties differ between a provider of a high-risk AI system, a deployer and the victim of a fraud. Do not assert that a duty applies; name the question and the plan to check. Reporting clocks come from the scenario configuration. Every customer, product and company is fictional.

decisionMustMention.description: the decision point involves pausing or rolling back the system, classifying the incident, evidence or a notice

addedThreatFamilies.label: Data poisoning and model tampering
addedThreatFamilies.description: Training data, a retrieval store or a model artifact has been corrupted or backdoored; the team investigates, rolls back and decides what to disclose.

phaseArc.title: Anomaly
phaseArc.goal: Behavior changes in a narrow, odd way.
beats: Outputs change only when a rare phrase appears
A retrieval store holds new documents from an unknown account
An evaluation score drops on one slice of cases

phaseArc.title: Investigation
phaseArc.goal: Find what changed, when and who touched it.
beats: Data lineage is incomplete for one source
A model artifact hash does not match the registry
The security team asks for a freeze on retraining

phaseArc.title: Rollback
phaseArc.goal: Return to a known good version without losing evidence.
beats: The last good model is two releases old
Retrieval content must be rebuilt from verified sources
Customers received outputs from the bad version for eleven days

phaseArc.title: Disclosure
phaseArc.goal: Decide what to tell customers, partners and regulators.
beats: Legal asks whether the event is a cyber incident with its own clocks
The vendor that supplied the data denies a breach
The review changes who may add data to the store

decisionPointExamples: roll back to an older model now, or keep serving while the investigation finishes
tell customers the outputs may have been affected before the scope is known, or wait
addedThreatFamilies.clueKinds: a hash mismatch against the registry, an unexplained slice-specific score drop, a new document source, access logs for the model store
addedThreatFamilies.hurdleKinds: missing data lineage, the registry was not enforced, the old model needs a library that is no longer supported
addedThreatFamilies.keyCoordination: the security team, the data supplier and legal
addedThreatFamilies.promptGuidance: Describe the technical signs at the level a responder needs: what changed, what to compare and who to call. Do not give instructions for poisoning a model. Everything is fictional.

decisionMustMention.description: the decision point involves rollback, a freeze, a disclosure or the vendor

addedThreatFamilies.label: AI vendor or supply chain breach
addedThreatFamilies.description: A model, data or tooling vendor is compromised or has an incident; the team finds out what it exposed, applies interim controls and meets its duties to its own customers.

phaseArc.title: Vendor notice
phaseArc.goal: A short, vague notice arrives.
beats: The vendor says "a limited number of customers" may be affected
The vendor status page says "degraded performance"
Procurement cannot find which contract clause covers notice

phaseArc.title: Scope check
phaseArc.goal: What of ours did the vendor hold or touch?
beats: Prompts and uploaded documents were sent to the vendor API
Keys issued to the vendor must be rotated
The AI system inventory is out of date

phaseArc.title: Interim controls
phaseArc.goal: Reduce exposure while facts arrive.
beats: Switching to a fallback model changes outputs
Customers ask whether their data was involved
The vendor questionnaire answers disagree with its notice

phaseArc.title: Duties and lessons
phaseArc.goal: Meet the clocks that apply to us.
beats: Privacy counsel asks which clock started and when
The board asks about concentration on one vendor
A contract review is opened

decisionPointExamples: cut the vendor integration now, or keep it while scope is unclear
notify customers on the vendor's partial notice, or wait for our own scope check
addedThreatFamilies.clueKinds: a vendor notice with no scope, an inventory entry naming the vendor and data classes sent, key rotation logs
addedThreatFamilies.hurdleKinds: no fallback model, a contract with no notice deadline, the vendor contact is a shared mailbox
addedThreatFamilies.keyCoordination: the vendor, procurement and privacy counsel
addedThreatFamilies.promptGuidance: Vendor and customer names are fictional. The vendor's first notice is short and incomplete, and stays so for a while.

decisionMustMention.description: the decision point involves the vendor, the contract, the inventory, keys or a customer notice

addedThreatFamilies.label: AI service degradation
addedThreatFamilies.description: The controls around AI quietly stop working: a monitoring blind spot, an evaluation pipeline that expired, a deepfake detector that is down. The team notices late and decides how much to trust what happened in between.

phaseArc.title: Quiet failure
phaseArc.goal: The signal that would have warned them is missing.
beats: An evaluation job has not run for nineteen days
The moderation queue is empty because intake broke
The detector returns a default score for every item

phaseArc.title: Discovery
phaseArc.goal: Someone asks why the dashboard is flat.
beats: A manual check finds the pipeline credential expired
The team must decide what the gap hides
A customer complaint arrives that the monitor should have caught

phaseArc.title: Backfill
phaseArc.goal: Reconstruct what was missed.
beats: Backfilled evaluations show the harmful-output rate rose after day six
The moderation queue now holds a backlog
Review of the detector log shows missed items

phaseArc.title: Repair and report
phaseArc.goal: Fix the control and decide who to tell.
beats: Add a heartbeat alert to every control
Decide whether the gap changes any earlier assessment
The board asks how many other controls are unmonitored

decisionPointExamples: assume nothing happened during the gap, or backfill and review before saying so
rerun every evaluation now, or prioritize the customer-facing system
addedThreatFamilies.clueKinds: a flat line where noise should be, a job with no recent run, a default value repeated
addedThreatFamilies.hurdleKinds: the owner of the pipeline left, no heartbeat alert, the backfill needs data that was not kept
addedThreatFamilies.keyCoordination: the model owner and the board
addedThreatFamilies.promptGuidance: A degradation is an absence of signal. Make the clue the missing data, with dates, never a dramatic event.

decisionMustMention.description: the decision point involves a backfill, monitoring, an evaluation or the detector

noiseExamples: a routine vendor invoice for an unrelated service
a marketing request to use the assistant in a campaign
an employee asking how to label a legitimate AI-generated slide
a customer asking why the chat window looks different
an auditor asking for last year's model inventory
pressureExamples: a bank saying the recall cutoff is in forty minutes
a reporter asking whether the clip is real before a 5 p.m. deadline
a board member asking if the regulator must be told today
the product owner asking not to pause a feature that drives sign-ups
the impersonated executive asking why the company has not answered publicly
